decks.title: The President — Part 1: Election, Impeachment and Powers
goals: State the qualifications of the President and describe the Electoral College
Give reasons for the indirect election and state the term of office
Describe the ground and procedure of impeachment
Explain the executive, legislative and financial powers of the President

slides.heading: The President and the Vice-President
slides.body_md: Part 1 — who becomes **President**, how the President is **elected** and **removed**, and what **powers** the office holds.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: who can become President, the Electoral College, why the election is indirect, impeachment, and the executive, legislative and financial powers
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: Every law in India is signed by one person, and every government order is issued in that person's name. That person is the President of India. Yet the President rarely takes decisions alone. In this chapter we find out who can become President, who votes in the election, how a President can be removed, and how the President's many powers are actually used.

slides.heading: Head of State and head of government
slides.body_md: India follows the **parliamentary** system: the President is the **head of State**, the Prime Minister the **head of government**.

rows: Elected indirectly by an Electoral College
Leader who commands a majority in the Lok Sabha
Real executive power with the Council of Ministers

visual.alt: Table contrasting the President as head of State, elected indirectly and acting on advice, with the Prime Minister as head of government who leads the majority and holds real power

slides.narration: India has two heads. The President is the head of State, the face of the nation and the name in which the government acts. The Prime Minister is the head of government, who leads the party or alliance with a majority in the Lok Sabha. Real executive power lies with the Prime Minister and the Council of Ministers, while the President acts on their advice.

slides.heading: Who can become President?
slides.body_md: Four conditions, set by the Constitution.

visual.alt: Table of qualifications: both offices need Indian citizenship, an age of at least 35 and no office of profit; the President must be qualified for the Lok Sabha and the Vice-President for the Rajya Sabha

slides.narration: To become President, a person must be a citizen of India, must have completed thirty-five years of age, and must be qualified to become a member of the Lok Sabha. The person must not hold an office of profit under the Union, a State or a local body. Offices such as minister or Governor do not count as offices of profit for this rule.

slides.heading: Quick check: two heads
slides.body_md: Which office is the head of State in India?
slides.narration: Remember the difference between the head of State and the head of government. Which one is the President?

slides.heading: The Electoral College
slides.body_md: Only **elected** legislators vote: Parliament, State Assemblies, and the Assemblies of **Delhi** and **Puducherry** (since **1992**).

visual.caption: Who votes for the President.

slides.narration: The President is not chosen by the people directly. An Electoral College votes instead. It has the elected members of both Houses of Parliament, the elected members of every State Legislative Assembly, and, since nineteen ninety-two, the elected members of the Delhi and Puducherry Assemblies. Nominated members and members of Legislative Councils have no vote. Voting is by the single transferable vote and a secret ballot.

slides.heading: Why an indirect election?
slides.body_md: The framers wanted a **constitutional head**, not a rival to the Prime Minister.

nodes.label: The President is a constitutional head
Direct election could create a rival centre of power
A nationwide campaign would cost time and money
State legislators give the States a voice

visual.alt: Flow of reasons for indirect election: the President is a constitutional head, direct election could create a rival to the Prime Minister, a national campaign would be costly, and State legislators give the States a voice
visual.caption: Four reasons to remember.

slides.narration: Why not let the people vote directly? First, the President is only a constitutional head, and a direct mandate might suggest real power. Second, a directly elected President might clash with the Prime Minister. Third, a nationwide campaign for a ceremonial office would be costly. Finally, including State legislators gives every State a voice, which suits a federal country.

slides.heading: Quick check: leaving office early
slides.body_md: To whom does a President write when resigning?
slides.narration: The President serves five years and can be re-elected. But who receives the letter if a President decides to resign early?

slides.heading: Worked example 1: who votes?
slides.body_md: Sort five imagined legislators.
bullets: Ask: is the member **elected**?
Ask: is the body **Parliament**, a **State Assembly**, or the **Delhi** or **Puducherry** Assembly?
Councils and nominated members are always **out**.

rows: Elected member of the Lok Sabha
Nominated member of the Rajya Sabha
Elected member of a State Assembly
Elected member of a State Assembly
Member of a State Legislative Council
Councils are not in the College
Elected member of the Delhi Assembly

visual.alt: Worked example table: elected members of Parliament, of State Assemblies and of the Delhi Assembly vote for the President; nominated members and Legislative Council members do not

slides.narration: Let us test the rule with five imagined legislators. An elected Lok Sabha member votes. A nominated Rajya Sabha member does not, because only elected members vote. An elected member of a State Assembly votes. A member of a State Legislative Council does not vote at all. An elected member of the Delhi Assembly votes, thanks to the change made in nineteen ninety-two.

slides.heading: Impeachment
slides.body_md: The only ground is **violation of the Constitution** (Article 61).

nodes.label: Notice signed by at least one-fourth of the members of one House, 14 days ahead
That House passes it by two-thirds of its total membership
The other House investigates; the President may defend himself
The other House also passes it by two-thirds: the President is removed

visual.alt: Flow of impeachment: a charge of violating the Constitution, notice signed by one-fourth of a House fourteen days ahead, passage by two-thirds of that House, investigation by the other House with a right of defence, and removal if the other House also passes it by two-thirds
visual.caption: Article 61.

slides.narration: A President can be removed before the end of the term only by impeachment, and only for violating the Constitution. Either House can start it. A notice signed by at least one-fourth of the members is given fourteen days ahead. That House must pass the charge by two-thirds of its total membership. The other House investigates, the President may defend himself, and a second two-thirds vote removes him.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: counting the votes
slides.body_md: Use the **total membership**, and round **up**.

visual.alt: Worked example table: with 543 members the Lok Sabha needs 136 signatures and 362 votes; with 245 members the Rajya Sabha needs 62 signatures and 164 votes
visual.caption: Counts are rounded up to whole members.

slides.narration: Let us count. In a Lok Sabha of five hundred and forty-three members, one-fourth is a little under one hundred and thirty-six, so at least one hundred and thirty-six must sign. Two-thirds is three hundred and sixty-two. In a Rajya Sabha of two hundred and forty-five, sixty-two must sign and one hundred and sixty-four must vote in favour. These large numbers protect the office.

slides.body_md: On what ground can impeachment begin?
slides.narration: There is only one ground for impeachment. Can you name it?

slides.heading: Executive powers
slides.body_md: All executive action is taken in the President's **name**.

rows: Prime Minister and ministers, judges, Governors, Attorney General, Comptroller and Auditor General
All executive action is taken in the President's name
Supreme Commander of the Army, Navy and Air Force
Ambassadors are sent and received in the President's name

visual.alt: Table of executive powers of the President: appointments of top officials, administration in his name, supreme command of the defence forces, and foreign affairs

slides.narration: The executive power of the Union belongs to the President. The President appoints the Prime Minister and, on his advice, the other ministers. Judges, Governors, the Attorney General and the Comptroller and Auditor General are also appointed by the President. The President is the Supreme Commander of the defence forces, and ambassadors act in the President's name. In practice, all this is done on the advice of the Council of Ministers.

slides.heading: Legislative powers
slides.body_md: The President is a **part of Parliament**.

rows: Summons and prorogues the Houses; dissolves the Lok Sabha
Speaks to both Houses after each general election and at the first session of each year
Names 12 members of the Rajya Sabha
Assents to bills, withholds assent or returns an ordinary bill once
Makes temporary laws when Parliament is not in session

visual.alt: Table of legislative powers: summoning, proroguing and dissolving, addressing both Houses, nominating twelve Rajya Sabha members, assent to bills and ordinances

slides.narration: Parliament consists of the President and the two Houses. The President summons and prorogues the Houses and can dissolve the Lok Sabha. The President addresses both Houses after each general election and at the first session every year, and nominates twelve members to the Rajya Sabha. No bill becomes law without the President's assent.

slides.heading: Three kinds of veto

rows: The bill does not become law
If passed again, assent must follow
The bill stays pending; no time limit is fixed

visual.alt: Table of the three vetoes: absolute (assent withheld), suspensive (an ordinary bill returned once, assent must follow if it is passed again) and pocket (no decision taken)

slides.narration: When a bill reaches the President, there are three ways to hold it back. Withholding assent is the absolute veto. Returning an ordinary bill once for reconsideration is the suspensive veto; if Parliament passes it again, the President must sign. Taking no decision at all is the pocket veto, possible because the Constitution sets no time limit.

slides.heading: Ordinances
slides.body_md: Temporary laws under **Article 123**, made only when Parliament is **not in session**.

visual.alt: Flow of an ordinance: Parliament not in session, urgent need with ministerial advice, the ordinance is issued, laid before Parliament when it meets, and lapses 6 weeks after reassembly unless approved
visual.caption: Article 123.

slides.narration: Sometimes a law is needed urgently while Parliament is not sitting. The President, on the advice of ministers, can issue an ordinance, which has the same force as a law of Parliament. It must be placed before Parliament when it meets again, and it stops working six weeks after Parliament reassembles unless it is approved.

slides.heading: Quick check: dissolving a House
slides.body_md: Which House can the President dissolve?
slides.narration: One House is permanent and one is not. Which House can the President dissolve?

slides.heading: Financial powers

rows: Introduced only on the President's recommendation
The annual financial statement is laid before Parliament in his name
Advances for unforeseen expenses before Parliament approves
Appointed every five years to advise on sharing revenue with the States

visual.alt: Table of financial powers: recommending Money Bills, causing the budget to be laid, advancing money from the Contingency Fund and appointing the Finance Commission

slides.narration: The President also has financial powers. A Money Bill can be introduced only on the President's recommendation. The budget is laid before Parliament in the President's name. In a sudden crisis, the President can make advances from the Contingency Fund of India. Every five years, the President appoints a Finance Commission to advise on how revenue is shared with the States.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1
bullets: Citizen, 35 years, qualified for the Lok Sabha, no office of profit.
Elected by elected MPs and elected members of State, Delhi and Puducherry Assemblies; five-year term; may be re-elected.
Impeachment only for violating the Constitution: one-fourth to sign, two-thirds of each House to pass.
Executive, legislative and financial powers are used on ministerial advice.

nodes.label: Impeachment by two-thirds of each House

visual.alt: Summary flow of Part 1: qualifications and indirect election, the Electoral College of elected legislators, impeachment by two-thirds of each House, and powers used on ministerial advice
visual.caption: Part 1 in four lines.

slides.narration: To sum up Part 1. The President must be a citizen, at least thirty-five, qualified for the Lok Sabha and free of any office of profit. Elected legislators form the Electoral College. Impeachment is possible only for violating the Constitution and needs two-thirds of each House. The President has wide executive, legislative and financial powers, but uses them on the advice of ministers.

slides.heading: Exam tips for Part 1
bullets: Do not include nominated members or Legislative Councils in the Electoral College.
Impeachment uses **two-thirds of the total membership**, not of members present.
Do not confuse the age for the Lok Sabha (25) with the President (35).
An ordinance lapses six weeks after Parliament **reassembles**.
10-mark answers: one clear point per mark in each part.
slides.narration: A few tips. Leave nominated members and Legislative Councils out of the Electoral College. For impeachment, say two-thirds of the total membership of each House. Keep the ages straight: twenty-five for the Lok Sabha, thirty-five for the President. Count the six weeks for an ordinance from the day Parliament reassembles. And in long answers, give one clear point for every mark.

decks.title: The President — Part 2: Mercy, Discretion, Emergencies and the Vice-President
goals: Explain the President's power to grant pardon, reprieve and remission
Identify situations in which the President may use discretion
Distinguish the three emergencies by ground and state two effects of each
Describe the qualifications, election, removal and roles of the Vice-President

slides.heading: Mercy, discretion, emergencies and the Vice-President
slides.body_md: Part 2 — the President's **judicial**, **discretionary** and **emergency** powers, and the office of the **Vice-President**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: the judicial powers of the President, the discretionary powers, the three kinds of emergency and the office of the Vice-President
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: In Part 1 we saw how the President is elected and the ordinary powers of the office. Now we turn to powers that come into play in special moments: showing mercy to a convict, choosing a Prime Minister when no party has a majority, and declaring an emergency. We end with the Vice-President, the second highest office in the country.

slides.heading: Judicial power: Article 72
slides.body_md: The President can show **mercy**, even in death-sentence and court-martial cases.

rows: Frees the convict from the sentence and its consequences
Changes the punishment into a lighter form
Shortens the period without changing the kind of punishment
Gives a lesser sentence because of a special fact, such as illness
Delays the carrying out of a sentence for a time

visual.alt: Table of the five forms of mercy under Article 72: pardon, commutation, remission, respite and reprieve, with the meaning of each

slides.narration: Under Article seventy-two, the President can grant mercy to a person convicted of an offence, acting on the advice of the government. There are five forms. A pardon frees the person completely. Commutation changes the punishment to a lighter kind. Remission shortens the period. A respite gives a lighter sentence for a special reason. A reprieve delays the sentence for a time.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: which form of mercy?
slides.body_md: Match each imagined case to the right word.

rows: A ten-year sentence is cut to six years
A sentence of hard labour becomes simple imprisonment
A hanging is delayed while a petition is heard
A pregnant convict is given a lighter sentence

visual.alt: Worked example table matching imagined cases to forms of mercy: a shortened term is remission, a lighter kind of punishment is commutation, a delay is a reprieve, and a lighter sentence for a special reason is a respite

slides.narration: Try four imagined cases. A ten-year sentence cut to six years is remission, because only the length changes. Hard labour turned into simple imprisonment is commutation, because the kind of punishment changes. A hanging delayed while a petition is heard is a reprieve. A lighter sentence for a pregnant convict is a respite.

slides.heading: Quick check: the Article
slides.body_md: Which Article gives the President the power of mercy?
slides.narration: Recall the Article number that gives the President the power to grant mercy.

slides.heading: Discretionary powers
slides.body_md: Not written as a list, but they arise in **situations**.

nodes.label: Hung Lok Sabha: choosing a Prime Minister
Seeking information from the Prime Minister

visual.alt: Flow of situations where the President uses some discretion: choosing a Prime Minister in a hung Lok Sabha, returning advice once, keeping a bill pending, and seeking information from the Prime Minister
visual.caption: Situational discretion.

slides.narration: The President usually acts on advice, but some situations leave room for judgement. If no party has a majority after an election, the President chooses the leader most likely to win the confidence of the Lok Sabha. The President can return advice once for reconsideration, keep a bill pending, and ask the Prime Minister for information about the government's work.

slides.heading: Advice: how the rule changed

nodes.label: 1950: Constitution provides a Council of Ministers to aid and advise
1978: 44th Amendment allows one return for reconsideration

visual.alt: Timeline flow on ministerial advice: in 1950 the Constitution provides a Council of Ministers to aid and advise; in 1976 the 42nd Amendment makes advice binding; in 1978 the 44th Amendment allows advice to be returned once
visual.caption: Article 74 over time.

slides.narration: Article seventy-four has changed over time. The original Constitution simply said there would be a Council of Ministers to aid and advise the President. In nineteen seventy-six, the forty-second Amendment made that advice binding. In nineteen seventy-eight, the forty-fourth Amendment added that the President may send the advice back once; after reconsideration, the President must act on it.

slides.heading: Three kinds of emergency
slides.body_md: Know the **Article**, the **ground**, the **approval period** and **two effects** of each.

rows: War, external aggression or armed rebellion
Failure of constitutional machinery in a State
Threat to financial stability or credit of India
Laws on State subjects; directions to States
Union runs the State; Parliament makes its laws
Salary cuts; State Money Bills reserved

visual.alt: Table comparing the three emergencies: Article 352 national emergency for war, aggression or armed rebellion, approved within one month; Article 356 President's Rule for failure of State machinery and Article 360 financial emergency for a financial threat, each approved within two months; with two effects of each

slides.narration: The Constitution provides three kinds of emergency. A national emergency, under Article three hundred and fifty-two, is for war, external aggression or armed rebellion. President's Rule, under Article three hundred and fifty-six, is for a breakdown of government in a State. A financial emergency, under Article three hundred and sixty, is for a threat to India's financial stability or credit.

slides.heading: National emergency
slides.body_md: Safeguards since **1978**: a **written** Cabinet decision and approval within **one month**.

nodes.label: Cabinet decides and informs the President in writing
Both Houses approve within 1 month by a special majority
Federal system works like a unitary one

visual.alt: Flow of a national emergency: the Cabinet's written decision, the proclamation, approval by both Houses within one month by special majority, and the federal system working like a unitary one
visual.caption: Safeguards added in 1978.

slides.narration: After the forty-fourth Amendment, the President can proclaim a national emergency only when the Cabinet's decision is given in writing, and both Houses must approve it within one month by a special majority. During the emergency, Parliament can make laws on State subjects and the Union can direct the States. The freedoms of Article nineteen can be suspended if the emergency is due to war or external aggression.

slides.heading: Quick check: a changed word
slides.body_md: Which words replaced "internal disturbance" in Article 352?
slides.narration: The forty-fourth Amendment narrowed one of the grounds for a national emergency. What is the new wording?

slides.heading: President's Rule in a State

nodes.label: Governor runs the State for the Union

visual.alt: Flow of President's Rule: the Governor reports a breakdown, the proclamation, approval by Parliament within 2 months, the Governor running the State for the Union, and the Assembly suspended or dissolved
visual.caption: Article 356.

slides.narration: When the government of a State cannot be carried on according to the Constitution, the President may take over. Usually the Governor sends a report first. Parliament must approve the proclamation within two months. The Governor then runs the State on behalf of the Union, Parliament makes laws for the State, and the State Assembly is suspended or dissolved.

slides.heading: Financial emergency
slides.body_md: Article 360 had never been used (as of 2024).

rows: Pay of Union and State employees and of judges may be reduced
May be reserved for the President's consideration
The Union may direct States to follow financial discipline

visual.alt: Table of effects of a financial emergency: salaries including those of judges may be cut, State Money Bills may be reserved for the President, and States may be directed to follow financial discipline

slides.narration: A financial emergency can be declared when the financial stability or credit of India is threatened. Parliament must approve it within two months. The Union can then order cuts in the salaries of government servants, including judges, and can require State Money Bills to be reserved for the President. This provision had never been used, as of twenty twenty-four.

slides.heading: Quick check: effects of Article 360
slides.body_md: Which is an effect of a financial emergency?
slides.narration: Think about money. Which of the options is an effect of a financial emergency?

slides.heading: The Vice-President
slides.body_md: Same age and term as the President, but chosen by **Parliament alone**.

rows: Elected MPs and elected members of State, Delhi and Puducherry Assemblies
Impeachment by two-thirds of each House
Rajya Sabha resolution by majority of all members, agreed by the Lok Sabha

slides.narration: The Vice-President must be a citizen, at least thirty-five, qualified for the Rajya Sabha, and free of any office of profit. sections.heading: 1. Qualifications, election and term
sections.body_md:
- **Qualifications:** citizen of India; completed **35 years**; qualified for election to the **Lok Sabha**; no **office of profit** (posts such as minister, Governor or Vice-President are not counted).
- **Electoral College:** **elected** members of both Houses of Parliament, **elected** members of State Legislative Assemblies and of the **Delhi** and **Puducherry** Assemblies (**70th Amendment, 1992**). Nominated members and Legislative Councils are excluded.
- **Method:** proportional representation by **single transferable vote**, secret ballot; the value of an MLA's vote depends on the State's population.
- **Why indirect:** constitutional head; no rival to the Prime Minister; cost of a national campaign; a voice for the States.
- **Term:** five years; may be re-elected; resignation is addressed to the Vice-President.

sections.heading: 2. Impeachment
sections.body_md:
- **Ground:** violation of the Constitution only (**Article 61**).
- **Notice:** in either House, signed by at least **one-fourth** of its total members, **14 days** in advance.
- **First House:** resolution passed by **two-thirds of its total membership**.
- **Second House:** investigates; the President may appear or be represented; if it also passes the resolution by two-thirds of its total membership, the President is removed.
- Nominated MPs **take part**; State legislators **do not**.

key_terms.definition_md: The quasi-judicial procedure by which Parliament removes a President for violating the Constitution.

sections.heading: 3. Executive, legislative and financial powers
sections.body_md:
- **Executive:** appoints the Prime Minister and ministers, judges, Governors, Attorney General, Comptroller and Auditor General, Election Commissioners; Supreme Commander of the defence forces.
- **Legislative:** summons and prorogues the Houses; dissolves the Lok Sabha; special address (Article 87); nominates **12** members to the Rajya Sabha; assent, withholding of assent or return of an ordinary bill once; **ordinances** under **Article 123**, which lapse six weeks after Parliament reassembles.
- **Financial:** recommendation for Money Bills; budget laid in his name; advances from the **Contingency Fund**; appoints the **Finance Commission** every five years.
- All are used on the **advice of the Council of Ministers** (Article 74).

sections.heading: 4. Judicial and discretionary powers
sections.body_md:
- **Article 72:** pardon, commutation, remission, respite and reprieve, including death sentences and court-martial cases.
- **Discretion (situational):** choosing a Prime Minister when no party has a majority; returning advice **once** for reconsideration (44th Amendment, 1978); the pocket veto; seeking information from the Prime Minister.
- The **42nd Amendment (1976)** made ministerial advice binding; the **44th** allowed one return.

sections.heading: 5. Emergency powers
sections.body_md:
- **Article 352 (national emergency):** war, external aggression or **armed rebellion**; written Cabinet decision; approval within **one month** by special majority. Effects: Parliament legislates on the **State List**; the Union directs States; Article 19 freedoms can be suspended in a war emergency; the Lok Sabha term can be extended one year at a time.
- **Article 356 (President's Rule):** failure of the constitutional machinery in a State; approval within **two months**. Effects: the Union takes over the State executive through the Governor; Parliament makes the State's laws; the Assembly is suspended or dissolved.
- **Article 360 (financial emergency):** threat to financial stability or credit; approval within **two months**. Effects: salary cuts including judges; State Money Bills reserved for the President. Never proclaimed (as of 2024).

sections.heading: 6. The Vice-President
sections.body_md:
- **Qualifications:** citizen; **35 years**; qualified for the **Rajya Sabha**; no office of profit.
- **Election:** all members of both Houses of Parliament, **elected and nominated**; single transferable vote, secret ballot; **five-year** term.
- **Removal:** resolution of the **Rajya Sabha** passed by a majority of all its then members and **agreed to by the Lok Sabha**; **14 days'** notice. No impeachment.
- **Roles:** ex-officio **Chairman of the Rajya Sabha** (not a member; casting vote in a tie); **acts as President** during a vacancy (to be filled within six months) or absence, and then does not preside over the Rajya Sabha.

**Common mistakes**
- Including nominated members or Legislative Councils in the presidential Electoral College.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: one correct option or term.
- 2 marks: two distinct points.
- 10-mark questions in 3 + 3 + 4 parts: one point per mark; the last part usually asks for a reason, a comparison or an evaluation.

questions.stem_md: What is the minimum age a citizen must have completed to be elected President of India?

options.text_md: 25 years
35 years
30 years
40 years

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** 35 years. The Constitution requires a presidential candidate to have completed 35 years. Twenty-five is the age for the Lok Sabha and thirty for the Rajya Sabha; forty is not a constitutional figure here.

questions.stem_md: Besides citizenship and age, a presidential candidate must be qualified to become a member of which body?

options.text_md: The Rajya Sabha
A State Legislative Council
The Supreme Court
The Lok Sabha

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The Lok Sabha. The President must be qualified for election as a member of the Lok Sabha. The Vice-President, by contrast, must be qualified for the Rajya Sabha. A Legislative Council and the Supreme Court are not mentioned in these qualifications.

questions.stem_md: Ravindran, an imagined senior officer drawing a salary as a district collector, wishes to file nomination papers for the office of President while staying in his job. What does the Constitution say?

options.text_md: He cannot be a candidate while holding an office of profit under the government
He may contest because collectors are exempt from all conditions
He may contest only if he is under 35 years of age
He may contest only after serving in the Rajya Sabha

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** He cannot be a candidate while holding an office of profit under the government. A person holding an office of profit under the Union, a State or a local authority cannot be elected President. Offices such as minister, Governor or Vice-President are not counted as offices of profit for this rule, but a salaried government post is. The other options invent conditions.

questions.stem_md: An imagined State has a Legislative Council as well as an Assembly. Which of its legislators take part in electing the President?

options.text_md: All members of both the Assembly and the Council
Only the members of the Legislative Council
Only the elected members of the Legislative Assembly
The nominated members of the Assembly and the Council

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Only the elected members of the Legislative Assembly. The Electoral College includes only the elected members of the State Legislative Assemblies (and of both Houses of Parliament, and of the Delhi and Puducherry Assemblies). Members of Legislative Councils and nominated members have no vote in this election.

questions.stem_md: A member nominated to the Rajya Sabha for her work in classical music wants to vote in the presidential election. Which statement is correct?

options.text_md: She can vote, because every member of Parliament votes
She can vote only if the Speaker allows it
She cannot vote, because only elected members of Parliament form part of the Electoral College
She can vote twice, once in each House

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** She cannot vote, because only elected members of Parliament form part of the Electoral College. Nominated members of either House are not part of the Electoral College for the President, so she has no vote. Only elected members vote, once each.

questions.stem_md: Which constitutional amendment added the elected members of the Legislative Assemblies of the National Capital Territory of Delhi and of Puducherry to the presidential Electoral College?

options.text_md: The 70th Amendment (1992)
The 42nd Amendment (1976)
The 44th Amendment (1978)
The 52nd Amendment (1985)

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The 70th Amendment (1992). The 70th Amendment, in force from 1992, brought these two Union Territory assemblies into the Electoral College. The 42nd and 44th Amendments dealt with ministerial advice and emergency provisions; the 52nd Amendment is the Anti-Defection Law.

questions.stem_md: A President decides to leave office before the five-year term ends. To whom must the letter of resignation be addressed?

options.text_md: The Prime Minister
The Chief Justice of India
The Speaker of the Lok Sabha
The Vice-President

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The Vice-President. The President resigns by writing addressed to the Vice-President, who then informs the Speaker of the Lok Sabha. The Prime Minister and the Chief Justice do not receive it.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The framers of the Constitution chose indirect election for the President rather than a direct vote by the people.

**Reason (R):** A directly elected President could claim a popular mandate of his own and come into conflict with a Prime Minister who also leads the elected majority.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: (A) is true and (R) is false.
(A) is false and (R) is true.
Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Both statements are true, and R gives a main reason for A: since real power lies with the Prime Minister and the Council of Ministers, a nominal head chosen by direct vote might rival them. Indirect election keeps the President a constitutional head.

questions.stem_md: True or false? A person who has completed a full term as President is eligible to be elected to the office again.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** The Constitution allows a President to be re-elected; it sets no limit on the number of terms.

questions.stem_md: The President holds office for a term of ___ years from the date of entering upon office.
questions.solution_md: The term is five years, though the President may resign earlier or be removed by impeachment.

questions.stem_md: Give two reasons why the Constitution provides for the indirect election of the President.
questions.solution_md: Any two valid reasons, e.g. nominal head, avoiding rivalry with the Prime Minister, cost, representation of the States.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. The President is only a **nominal (constitutional) head**; a direct election would suggest **real power** and could cause **conflict with the Prime Minister**.
2. A nationwide direct election would be **costly and time-consuming** for a largely ceremonial office.

questions.stem_md: Name the groups of legislators whose votes make up the Electoral College for the President.
questions.solution_md: Parliament (elected), State Assemblies (elected), Delhi and Puducherry Assemblies (elected).

answer.model_answer_md: The **elected members of both Houses of Parliament**, the **elected members of the State Legislative Assemblies**, and the **elected members of the Legislative Assemblies of Delhi and Puducherry**.

marking_scheme.step: Elected members of both Houses of Parliament
Elected members of State Assemblies and of the Delhi and Puducherry Assemblies

questions.stem_md: Explain why including the elected members of the State Legislative Assemblies in the Electoral College suits a federal country like India.
questions.solution_md: Three points linking State participation to federalism and to the President's national role.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. The President is the head of the **whole Union**, which includes the **States**, so the States should have a say in choosing him.
2. Including MLAs makes the President a representative of the **nation and the States**, not only of the party that controls Parliament.
3. It reflects the **federal** principle and gives the office **wider acceptance** across regions.

marking_scheme.step: Head of the Union including the States
Not only the choice of the party in Parliament

questions.stem_md: On what ground can impeachment proceedings be started against the President of India?

options.text_md: Losing a vote in the Rajya Sabha
Violation of the Constitution
Disagreement with the Prime Minister
Completion of five years in office

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Violation of the Constitution. Impeachment is possible only for violation of the Constitution. Votes in the Rajya Sabha, disagreements with the Prime Minister or the end of the term do not lead to impeachment.

questions.stem_md: Members of an imagined Lok Sabha with a total membership of 543 wish to bring an impeachment charge against the President. What is the least number of members who must sign the written notice?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** 136. The notice must be signed by at least one-fourth of the total members of the House: one-fourth of 543 is 135.75, so at least 136 members. 362 is the two-thirds needed to pass the resolution; 272 is a simple majority of the House; 50 is the support needed for some motions, not for impeachment.

questions.stem_md: After the notice period, an impeachment resolution is put to the vote in an imagined Rajya Sabha of 245 members. What is the least number of votes needed for it to pass in that House?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** 164. The resolution must be passed by not less than two-thirds of the total membership of the House: two-thirds of 245 is 163.33, so at least 164 votes. 123 would be a majority of all members, 62 is the one-fourth needed for the notice, and 245 is the whole House.

questions.stem_md: Which group of legislators has no vote in electing the President but does take part in impeaching the President?

options.text_md: Elected members of the State Legislative Assemblies
Members of the State Legislative Councils
Nominated members of both Houses of Parliament
Elected members of the Delhi Assembly

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Nominated members of both Houses of Parliament. Impeachment is carried out by Parliament as a whole, so nominated members of both Houses vote on it though they do not vote in the election. Elected MLAs (including Delhi's) vote in the election but not in impeachment; Legislative Council members take part in neither.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Members of the State Legislative Assemblies vote on the resolution to impeach the President.

**Reason (R):** Elected members of the State Legislative Assemblies are part of the Electoral College that elects the President.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: (A) is true and (R) is false.
(A) is false and (R) is true.
Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** A is false: impeachment takes place only in the two Houses of Parliament. R is true: elected MLAs do help elect the President.

questions.stem_md: Arrange the steps of the impeachment of a President in the correct order.

options.text_md: That House passes the charge by two-thirds of its total membership
The other House also passes the resolution by two-thirds of its total membership, and the President is removed
Written notice signed by at least one-fourth of the members of one House is given 14 days in advance
The other House investigates the charge, and the President may appear or be represented

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (c) → (a) → (d) → (b). Notice and fourteen days' gap; resolution in the first House by two-thirds; investigation by the other House with the President's right to defend; second two-thirds vote, after which the President stands removed.

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md: State two features of the impeachment procedure that make it difficult to remove a President for political reasons.
questions.solution_md: Any two: special majority in both Houses, 14 days' notice signed by one-fourth, investigation by the other House, right of defence, only ground is violation of the Constitution.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. A resolution needs **two-thirds of the total membership** of **each** House, not just a simple majority.
2. The President has the **right to appear and defend** himself while the **other House investigates** the charge.

questions.stem_md: The executive power of the Union is vested in the President. In practice, how is most of this power exercised?

options.text_md: By the President alone, without consulting anyone
By the Chief Justice on the President's behalf
By the Speaker of the Lok Sabha
On the advice of the Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** On the advice of the Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister. Article 74 provides a Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister to aid and advise the President, and the President acts on this advice. The other options describe no constitutional arrangement.

questions.stem_md: Which of these officials is appointed by the President?

options.text_md: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha
The Chief Minister of a State
The Chairman of a District Council
The Comptroller and Auditor General of India

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The Comptroller and Auditor General of India. The President appoints the Comptroller and Auditor General, as well as judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts, Governors and the Attorney General. The Speaker is elected by the Lok Sabha, a Chief Minister is appointed by the Governor, and district bodies have their own procedures.

questions.stem_md: The President is the Supreme Commander of the defence forces. Which statement about this power is correct?

options.text_md: The President personally commands troops in battle
The defence chiefs need no approval of the government
Decisions such as declaring war are taken by the President subject to Parliament's laws and on ministerial advice
Only the Rajya Sabha can control the defence forces

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Decisions such as declaring war are taken by the President subject to Parliament's laws and on ministerial advice. The supreme command is exercised in the President's name, regulated by law and on the advice of the Council of Ministers. The President does not lead troops, the chiefs work under the government, and both Houses (not only the Rajya Sabha) control defence through laws and money.

questions.stem_md: Parliament is not in session when an imagined outbreak of a cattle disease calls for an urgent law on movement of animals. Which power can the President use?

options.text_md: Declare a financial emergency
Issue an ordinance under Article 123
Dissolve the Rajya Sabha
Pardon the farmers in advance

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Issue an ordinance under Article 123. When either House is not in session and immediate action is needed, the President may issue an ordinance, which has the force of law. A financial emergency, dissolving the permanent Rajya Sabha or advance pardons do not fit the situation.

questions.stem_md: An ordinance was issued while Parliament was in recess. Parliament reassembles on 3 August and takes no action on it. When does the ordinance cease to operate?

options.text_md: At the end of 6 weeks from the reassembly of Parliament
Immediately on 3 August
After six months from the date it was issued
It never lapses unless the President withdraws it

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** At the end of 6 weeks from the reassembly of Parliament. An ordinance must be laid before both Houses and lapses at the end of 6 weeks from their reassembly unless approved earlier (or disapproved by resolutions). It does not end on the first day, it is not tied to six months from issue, and it cannot run indefinitely.

questions.stem_md: A President receives an ordinary bill passed by Parliament and simply keeps it pending for many months without giving assent, refusing assent or returning it. Which veto is this?

options.text_md: Suspensive veto
Pocket veto
Absolute veto
Qualified veto

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Pocket veto. The Constitution fixes no time limit for the President's decision on an ordinary bill, so keeping it pending is called the pocket veto. Returning it once is the suspensive veto; refusing assent is the absolute veto; a qualified veto (override by special majority) is not part of the Indian system.

questions.stem_md: Which financial power belongs to the President?

options.text_md: The President alone decides the rates of income tax
The President can spend from the Consolidated Fund without Parliament's approval for any purpose
The President approves State budgets before they are presented
A Money Bill can be introduced in the Lok Sabha only on the President's recommendation

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A Money Bill can be introduced in the Lok Sabha only on the President's recommendation. The President's prior recommendation is needed for a Money Bill, and the annual financial statement is laid in his name. Tax rates are fixed by Parliament's law; spending from the Consolidated Fund needs Parliament's approval; State budgets are not approved by the President in normal times.

questions.stem_md: A sudden cyclone strikes an imagined coastal region and the government needs money before Parliament can approve the spending. From which fund can the President make an advance?

options.text_md: The Contingency Fund of India
The Provident Fund of government employees
The State Disaster Fund of a different State
The Consolidated Fund of a State

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The Contingency Fund of India. The Contingency Fund of India is placed at the disposal of the President to meet unforeseen expenditure, pending approval by Parliament. The other funds are not under the President's control for this purpose.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The President may return a Money Bill to the Lok Sabha for reconsideration, as with an ordinary bill.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** A Money Bill is introduced with the President's own recommendation, so it is not returned for reconsideration; the President normally gives assent. Only an ordinary bill can be returned once.

questions.stem_md: Match each kind of presidential veto with the action that shows it.

options.text_md: Absolute veto
Suspensive veto
Pocket veto

match_right.text_md: Keeping a bill pending without any decision
Returning an ordinary bill once for reconsideration

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(p), (b)–(r), (c)–(q). Absolute: assent withheld. Suspensive: returned once; if Parliament passes it again, the President must assent. Pocket: no decision, because no time limit is fixed.

questions.stem_md: On which two occasions does the President address both Houses of Parliament assembled together?
questions.solution_md: Special address under Article 87: after each general election and at the first session of each year.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. At the start of the **first session after each general election** to the Lok Sabha.
2. At the start of the **first session of each year**.

questions.stem_md: What is an ordinance? State the condition under which the President can issue one.
questions.solution_md: Meaning; recess condition and urgency.

answer.model_answer_md: An ordinance is a **temporary law** made by the President that has the **same force as an Act of Parliament**. It can be issued only when **one or both Houses are not in session** and the President is satisfied that **immediate action** is needed.

marking_scheme.step: Condition: Parliament not in session and urgency

questions.stem_md: Mention three executive powers of the President.
questions.solution_md: Any three executive powers.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Appoints the **Prime Minister** and, on his advice, the **other ministers**.
2. Appoints high officials such as **judges** of the Supreme Court and High Courts, **Governors**, the **Attorney General** and the **Comptroller and Auditor General**.
3. Is the **Supreme Commander** of the defence forces; all executive action is taken in his **name**.

questions.stem_md: Under which Article can the President grant pardons, reprieves, respites or remissions of punishment?

options.text_md: Article 123
Article 352
Article 72
Article 61

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Article 72. Article 72 gives the President this judicial power, including in cases of the death sentence and court-martial. Article 123 is about ordinances, 352 about national emergency, and 61 about impeachment.

questions.stem_md: A prisoner in an imagined case has been sentenced to death. On the advice of the government, the President changes the punishment to life imprisonment. Which form of the power is this?

options.text_md: Respite
Reprieve
Commutation
Remission

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Commutation. Commutation replaces one form of punishment with a lighter form. A reprieve postpones a sentence for a time; a respite gives a lesser sentence for special reasons such as illness; remission reduces the period of a sentence without changing its nature.

questions.stem_md: After an imagined general election, no party or pre-election alliance has a majority in the Lok Sabha. Which presidential power becomes important?

options.text_md: The discretion to choose a Prime Minister who seems most likely to win the confidence of the House
The power to declare a national emergency
The power to issue an ordinance on taxes
The power to grant a pardon

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The discretion to choose a Prime Minister who seems most likely to win the confidence of the House. When no one clearly commands a majority, the President uses discretion (situational discretion) to invite the leader most likely to prove a majority, often asking for a vote of confidence within a time. The other powers are unrelated to forming a government.

questions.stem_md: Under the provision added by the 44th Amendment (1978), what may the President do when given advice by the Council of Ministers?

options.text_md: Reject the advice as often as he likes
Refer the advice to the Supreme Court for approval every time
Accept the advice only if the Rajya Sabha agrees
Ask the Council to reconsider the advice once; he must act on the advice given after reconsideration

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Ask the Council to reconsider the advice once; he must act on the advice given after reconsideration. The 42nd Amendment (1976) made ministerial advice binding; the 44th Amendment added that the President may send it back once for reconsideration, but must act on the reconsidered advice. The other options have no constitutional basis.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The President of India has some situational discretion in choosing a Prime Minister.

**Reason (R):** The President is elected indirectly by an Electoral College.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: (A) is true and (R) is false.
(A) is false and (R) is true.
Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Both statements are true, but R does not explain A. The discretion arises from situations such as a hung Lok Sabha, not from the method of election.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between a reprieve and a remission granted by the President.
questions.solution_md: Postponement versus reduction of the term.

answer.model_answer_md: A **reprieve** **postpones** the carrying out of a sentence (especially a death sentence) for a time. A **remission** **reduces the period** of a sentence without changing its character.

questions.stem_md: Give two situations in which the President can act with some discretion rather than simply follow advice.
questions.solution_md: Any two recognised situations.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Choosing a **Prime Minister** when **no party has a clear majority** in the Lok Sabha.
2. **Returning** the Council of Ministers' advice **once for reconsideration**, or keeping an ordinary bill pending (**pocket veto**).

questions.stem_md: The President is often called a constitutional or nominal head. Explain this description, and say why the office still matters.
questions.solution_md: Meaning of nominal head, with a reasoned note on why the office still matters.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. The President has wide powers on paper, but **exercises them on the advice** of the Council of Ministers, which holds **real power** (Article 74).
2. Hence he is the **head of State** while the Prime Minister is the **head of government**.
3. The office still matters: it gives **continuity**, can **return advice** once, uses **discretion** in a hung House, and acts as a **guardian of the Constitution**.

marking_scheme.step: Head of State versus head of government

questions.stem_md: On which of these grounds can a national emergency be proclaimed under Article 352 today?

options.text_md: Failure of the monsoon in several States
War, external aggression or armed rebellion
A fall in the value of the rupee
Defeat of the government in the Lok Sabha

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** War, external aggression or armed rebellion. Article 352 allows a proclamation for war, external aggression or armed rebellion; the 44th Amendment replaced "internal disturbance" with "armed rebellion". Droughts, currency changes and the defeat of a government are not grounds.

questions.stem_md: Since the 44th Amendment, what must the President receive before proclaiming a national emergency?

options.text_md: The decision of the Union Cabinet communicated to him in writing
An oral request from the Prime Minister
A resolution of all State Assemblies
A judgment of the Supreme Court

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The decision of the Union Cabinet communicated to him in writing. The President can proclaim a national emergency only after the Cabinet's decision is communicated to him in writing. An oral request is not enough, and State Assemblies or the Supreme Court are not involved in the proclamation.

questions.stem_md: The Governor of an imagined State reports that no party can form a stable government and the State cannot be run according to the Constitution. Which provision may be used?

options.text_md: National emergency under Article 352
President's Rule under Article 356
Financial emergency under Article 360
Impeachment under Article 61

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** President's Rule under Article 356. Article 356 applies when the constitutional machinery fails in a State, on the Governor's report or otherwise. Article 352 is for war, aggression or armed rebellion, Article 360 for a financial crisis, and Article 61 for removing the President.

questions.stem_md: Which is an effect of a financial emergency under Article 360?

options.text_md: The Lok Sabha is dissolved automatically
Fundamental Rights under Article 19 are suspended
Salaries of government servants, including judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts, may be reduced
The President takes over the functions of every State government

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Salaries of government servants, including judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts, may be reduced. During a financial emergency the Union can order cuts in salaries, including those of judges, and may require State Money Bills to be reserved for the President. Dissolution, suspension of Article 19 and taking over State governments are not effects of Article 360.

questions.stem_md: Three proclamations are made in an imagined year: a national emergency, President's Rule in a State, and a financial emergency. Within what period must each be approved by both Houses of Parliament?

options.text_md: Two months for all three
Six months for all three
One month for President's Rule only; the others need no approval
1 month for the national emergency; 2 months each for President's Rule and the financial emergency

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** 1 month for the national emergency; 2 months each for President's Rule and the financial emergency. A national emergency must be approved within 1 month (since the 44th Amendment), while President's Rule and a financial emergency must be approved within 2 months. Every proclamation needs Parliament's approval.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** During a national emergency declared on the ground of war, the freedoms in Article 19 can be suspended.

**Reason (R):** Article 358 allows the State to make laws restricting those freedoms while such an emergency is in force.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: (A) is true and (R) is false.
(A) is false and (R) is true.
Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Both are true and R explains A: Article 358 removes the protection of Article 19 during an emergency declared on the ground of war or external aggression.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A financial emergency under Article 360 had never been proclaimed in India (as of 2024).

**Reason (R):** Article 360 can be used whenever a State government loses its majority.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: (A) is true and (R) is false.
(A) is false and (R) is true.
Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** A is true as of 2024. R is false: Article 360 is for a threat to the financial stability or credit of India; a State government losing its majority may lead to Article 356, not 360.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Under President's Rule, Parliament may make laws on State subjects for that State, and the State Assembly may be suspended or dissolved.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** Under Article 356 the State's legislative powers are exercised by or under the authority of Parliament, and the Assembly may be kept in suspended animation or dissolved.

questions.stem_md: The 44th Amendment replaced the words "internal disturbance" in Article 352 with the words "armed ___".
questions.solution_md: Since 1978 the ground is "armed rebellion", which is narrower than the earlier "internal disturbance".

questions.stem_md: Match each emergency provision with its ground.

options.text_md: Article 352
Article 356
Article 360

match_right.text_md: Threat to the financial stability or credit of India
Failure of constitutional machinery in a State
War, external aggression or armed rebellion

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(q), (c)–(p). 352: national emergency; 356: President's Rule in a State; 360: financial emergency.

questions.stem_md: State two effects of a proclamation of national emergency on the federal structure.
questions.solution_md: Any two federal effects (State List laws, directions, change in distribution of revenues, extension of Lok Sabha term).

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Parliament** can make laws on subjects in the **State List**.
2. The Union can give **directions** to the States on how to use their executive power, so the system becomes nearly **unitary**.

questions.stem_md: Mention two effects of President's Rule in a State.
questions.solution_md: Executive taken over; legislative power with Parliament.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. The **President** takes over the **executive functions** of the State, usually exercised through the **Governor**.
2. **Parliament** makes laws for the State, while the **State Assembly** is suspended or dissolved.

questions.stem_md: Compare a national emergency with a financial emergency on three points.
questions.solution_md: Ground, approval period, effects.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Ground:** a national emergency is for **war, external aggression or armed rebellion**; a financial emergency for a threat to **financial stability or credit**.
2. **Approval:** within **one month** for a national emergency; within **two months** for a financial emergency.
3. **Effects:** a national emergency lets Parliament legislate on the **State List** and can suspend **Article 19**; a financial emergency allows **salary cuts** and control of State **Money Bills**.

questions.stem_md: Of which House is the Vice-President the ex-officio Chairman?

options.text_md: The Lok Sabha
Both Houses in turn
The State Legislative Council of his home State
The Rajya Sabha

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The Rajya Sabha. The Vice-President is the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha. The Lok Sabha has its own Speaker, there is no rotation, and State Councils have their own Chairmen.

questions.stem_md: Who elects the Vice-President?

options.text_md: Only elected members of Parliament and of the State Assemblies
Only the members of the Rajya Sabha
All members of both Houses of Parliament, elected and nominated
The people of India by direct vote

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** All members of both Houses of Parliament, elected and nominated. The Vice-President is elected by an Electoral College of all members of both Houses of Parliament, including nominated members, by proportional representation (single transferable vote, secret ballot). State legislators do not take part.

questions.stem_md: Members in an imagined Rajya Sabha of 245 members move a resolution to remove the Vice-President after the required notice. What must happen for the removal to take effect?

options.text_md: Two-thirds of the members of each House vote for it, as in impeachment
At least 123 members of the Rajya Sabha vote for it, and the Lok Sabha then agrees to it
The President dismisses the Vice-President on the Prime Minister's advice
The Supreme Court declares the Vice-President unfit

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** At least 123 members of the Rajya Sabha vote for it, and the Lok Sabha then agrees to it. The resolution must be passed in the Rajya Sabha by a majority of all its then members (an effective majority: here at least 123 of 245) and agreed to by the Lok Sabha. There is no impeachment for the Vice-President, no dismissal by the President and no court procedure.

questions.stem_md: The office of President falls vacant suddenly in an imagined year. What happens until a new President is elected?

options.text_md: The Vice-President acts as President, and the election must be held within six months
The Prime Minister acts as President for the remaining term
The Speaker of the Lok Sabha becomes President for five years
The office remains vacant until the next general election

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The Vice-President acts as President, and the election must be held within six months. The Vice-President discharges the functions of the President, and an election to fill the vacancy must be held within six months. The Prime Minister and the Speaker do not take over the office.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** While acting as President, the Vice-President does not perform the duties of Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.

**Reason (R):** The Vice-President is an elected member of the Rajya Sabha.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: (A) is true and (R) is false.
(A) is false and (R) is true.
Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** A is true: the Deputy Chairman presides while the Vice-President acts as President. R is false: the Vice-President is not a member of either House.

questions.stem_md: True or false? To be elected Vice-President, a citizen must be at least 35 years old and qualified for election to the Rajya Sabha.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** Both conditions are correct, along with not holding an office of profit.

questions.stem_md: State any two qualifications for election to the office of Vice-President.
questions.solution_md: Any two qualifications.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Must be a **citizen of India** who has completed **35 years**.
2. Must be **qualified for election to the Rajya Sabha** and must **not hold an office of profit**.

questions.stem_md: Describe two roles of the Vice-President of India.
questions.solution_md: Chairman role and acting President.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. As ex-officio **Chairman of the Rajya Sabha**, he **presides** over its sittings and keeps order; he has a **casting vote** in a tie.
2. He **acts as President** when the office falls vacant or when the President cannot work through absence or illness.

questions.stem_md: Compare the election of the President with that of the Vice-President on three points.
questions.solution_md: Three clear points of comparison.

answer.model_answer_md:

questions.stem_md:
An imagined student council wants to copy the way India elects its President.

(i) State three qualifications for election as President. **[3]**
(ii) Name the members who form the Electoral College and those who are left out. **[3]**
(iii) Explain four reasons why the President is elected indirectly. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Qualifications; members included and excluded; four reasons for indirect election.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) The candidate must be a **citizen of India**, must have completed **35 years**, must be **qualified for election to the Lok Sabha**, and must **not hold an office of profit** under the government.

(ii) The Electoral College consists of the **elected members of both Houses of Parliament**, the **elected members of the State Legislative Assemblies**, and the **elected members of the Delhi and Puducherry Assemblies**. **Nominated members** of Parliament and of the Assemblies, and members of **Legislative Councils**, are left out.

(iii) The President is a **nominal head**, and direct election would suggest **real power**. A directly elected President might **rival the Prime Minister**. A nationwide campaign would be **costly**. Including MLAs gives the **States** a voice, which suits **federalism**.

questions.stem_md:
Read the situation and answer. *(Imagined.)* Opposition members in the Lok Sabha accuse a President of acting against the Constitution.

(i) On what ground can a President be impeached, and in which House can the charge be brought? **[3]**
(ii) Explain how the charge is framed and passed in the House where it begins. **[3]**
(iii) Describe what happens in the second House and why the procedure is considered difficult. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Ground and House; notice and special majority; investigation, removal and why difficult.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) The only ground is **violation of the Constitution**. The charge can be brought in **either House** of Parliament.

(ii) A **written notice** signed by at least **one-fourth of the total members** of the House is given **14 days** in advance. The resolution must then be passed by **not less than two-thirds of the total membership** of that House.

(iii) The **other House investigates** the charge; the President has the right to **appear or be represented**. If that House also passes the resolution by **two-thirds of its total membership**, the President is **removed** from that date. The procedure is difficult because it needs a **special majority in both Houses**, a long **notice period** and a **fair hearing**.

marking_scheme.step: (iii) Second two-thirds vote, removal and why difficult

questions.stem_md:
The President is part of Parliament.

(i) Mention three legislative powers of the President connected with the meetings of Parliament. **[3]**
(ii) Explain the President's options when an ordinary bill passed by both Houses is sent for assent. **[3]**
(iii) What is an ordinance? State its duration and two limits on this power. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Meeting-related powers; veto options; ordinance meaning, duration and limits.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) The President **summons** and **prorogues** the Houses, can **dissolve the Lok Sabha**, **addresses** both Houses at the first session after a general election and each year, and may summon a **joint sitting**.

(ii) He may **give assent**, **withhold assent** (absolute veto) or **return the bill once** for reconsideration (suspensive veto); if Parliament passes it again, he **must assent**. Because no time limit is fixed, he may also keep it pending (**pocket veto**).

(iii) An ordinance is a **temporary law** made by the President when Parliament is **not in session** and immediate action is needed (Article 123). It lapses **six weeks after Parliament reassembles** unless approved. Limits: it can be made only on subjects on which **Parliament can make laws**, it is issued on the **advice of the ministers**, and it may be **reviewed by courts**.

marking_scheme.step: (ii) Assent, withhold, return; must assent if repassed

questions.stem_md:
Answer the following about the President's powers.

(i) Explain three financial powers of the President. **[3]**
(ii) Under Article 72, what kinds of mercy can the President grant? Explain any three. **[3]**
(iii) "The President of India is not a mere rubber stamp." Evaluate this statement with reference to his discretionary powers. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Financial powers; forms of mercy; balanced evaluation of discretion.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) A **Money Bill** can be introduced only on his **recommendation**; the **annual financial statement** is laid before Parliament on his behalf; he can make **advances from the Contingency Fund** for unforeseen expenses; he appoints a **Finance Commission** every five years.

(ii) He can grant a **pardon** (frees the person from the sentence), a **commutation** (a lighter form of punishment), a **remission** (shorter period) and a **reprieve** (postponement), including for the **death sentence**.

(iii) He normally acts on **ministerial advice** (Article 74), so most powers are formal. But he can **return advice once** for reconsideration (44th Amendment), use the **pocket veto**, and use **discretion in choosing a Prime Minister** when no party has a majority. These give him a real, though limited, role as a **guardian of the Constitution**, so he is more than a rubber stamp.

questions.stem_md:
The Constitution gives the President three kinds of emergency powers.

(i) State the ground of each kind of emergency and the Article under which it is proclaimed. **[3]**
(ii) Mention any two effects of a national emergency and one safeguard added by the 44th Amendment. **[3]**
(iii) Give two effects each of President's Rule and of a financial emergency. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Grounds and Articles; national emergency effects and safeguard; effects of the other two.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **National emergency (Article 352):** war, external aggression or armed rebellion. **President's Rule (Article 356):** failure of the constitutional machinery in a State. **Financial emergency (Article 360):** a threat to the financial stability or credit of India.

(ii) Effects: **Parliament can legislate on State List** subjects, the Union can **direct the States**, and Article **19 freedoms** can be suspended in a war emergency. Safeguard: the proclamation needs the **Cabinet's written decision** and approval by Parliament **within one month** by a special majority.

(iii) **President's Rule:** the President takes over the State's **executive** through the Governor; **Parliament** makes laws for the State and the Assembly is suspended or dissolved. **Financial emergency:** **salaries** of government servants and judges can be **cut**; State **Money Bills** may be reserved for the President.

questions.stem_md:
Answer the following about the Vice-President of India.

(i) State three qualifications for the office. **[3]**
(ii) Explain how the Vice-President is elected and removed. **[3]**
(iii) Describe the functions of the Vice-President as Chairman of the Rajya Sabha and as acting President. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Qualifications; election and removal; functions.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) A **citizen of India**, at least **35 years** old, **qualified for election to the Rajya Sabha**, and **not holding an office of profit**.

(ii) Elected by an Electoral College of **all members of both Houses** of Parliament, elected and nominated, by **proportional representation by single transferable vote** and **secret ballot**, for **five years**. Removed by a **Rajya Sabha resolution** passed by a **majority of all its then members** and **agreed to by the Lok Sabha**, after **14 days' notice**.

(iii) As **Chairman**, he **presides** over the Rajya Sabha, keeps **order**, decides points of procedure and has a **casting vote** in a tie. When the President's office is **vacant** or the President is **absent or ill**, he **acts as President** (a vacancy must be filled within six months); during that time he does **not preside** over the Rajya Sabha.

questions.stem_md:
The executive power of the Union is vested in the President.

(i) Mention three appointments made by the President. **[3]**
(ii) Explain what is meant by the President's role as Supreme Commander of the defence forces. **[3]**
(iii) Why is the President bound to act on the advice of the Council of Ministers? Refer to the 42nd and 44th Amendments. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Appointments; Supreme Commander; binding advice with the two amendments.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) The **Prime Minister** and other **ministers**, **judges** of the Supreme Court and High Courts, **Governors** of States, the **Attorney General**, the **Comptroller and Auditor General** and the **Election Commissioners**.

(ii) The defence forces are commanded in the **President's name**; he can **declare war or make peace**, but these powers are **regulated by Parliament's laws** and used on the **advice of the government**.

(iii) India has a **parliamentary system**: the **Council of Ministers** is responsible to the Lok Sabha, so it holds **real power** and must advise the President (Article 74). The **42nd Amendment (1976)** made this advice **binding**. The **44th Amendment (1978)** allowed the President to **return advice once** for reconsideration, after which he must act on it.

marking_scheme.step: (ii) In his name, regulated by law and advice
